doc.title: Henry Johnson interviewed by Michael Woods, Majesty of the Seas, May 30, 1995

title: Live playing versus perfect records
summary: Woods and Johnson prefer live playing; Johnson says modern perfect records are not musical, unlike 1950s-60s takes without overdubs.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Making records: studios, takes and the technology

blocks.x: You know the reason why I like it live is because you know in a recording studio if you make a mistake you can always either just take it again, or erase — keep everybody else’s good part and erase the guitar track for eight bars and then punch that back in or whatever you know. But I like it live when you count it off, you know you can’t stop, even if you get out there burning taking some solo and get yourself painted into a corner, you’ve still got to get out of it, and get back into that chorus and hand the ball back to somebody else.

And see the thing too is the recording industry has changed to make perfect records. And perfect records are not musical. Because you work on this thing until, you know, eight bars okay now I got to go to the next eight bars. And that’s really not a solo, that’s not anything that you feel. That’s something that you put together, you know, note by note. And you don’t put solos together note by note because those are the experiences. You don’t put those together note by note. The older, in the 50s and the 60s when they were recording records, you know there was no overdubs, you know. There was only four track recording, there was no overdubs. You do another take. And if you don’t like that take, you’re stuck with it. That’s it.
I even heard one musician say, he said if you don’t have it after three takes, that’s it. You just take the best of the three.
Yeah. And usually the first one is the one everybody goes for.
